{"id": "1d77ec6f-1fe6-4f61-b315-a07813a14986", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "AWS Config recording mode cost comparison guide"}]}

{"id": "82ee09e2-c6e1-46b2-9451-750c3a4342fc", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "For a resource type that changes many times per day, **daily recording is almost always cheaper** — and it's not close.

**Why:**

AWS Config bills per **configuration item (CI)** recorded, not per API call or per resource.

- **Continuous recording** creates a new configuration item every time the resource's configuration changes — so if a resource changes 20 times a day, you get 20 billable CIs for that resource that day.
- **Daily recording** creates at most **one configuration item per resource per day**, capturing the latest state regardless of how many times it changed in between.

So for a high-churn resource type (e.g., something like ECS task definitions, EC2 instances behind autoscaling, or frequently-updated security groups), continuous recording multiplies your CI count — and therefore your bill — by however many times that resource changes per day. Daily recording flattens that to a constant 1 CI/resource/day, regardless of churn.

**The tradeoff:** you lose the intra-day change history — daily recording only gives you the end-of-day snapshot, not every intermediate state. So it's a cost-vs-granularity decision:
- If you need to know about every individual change (for compliance audit trails, security investigations, etc.), continuous is worth the extra cost.
- If you just need periodic drift/compliance snapshots and don't care about every intermediate change, daily recording is the cheaper choice for high-churn resource types.

If you want, I can look at your actual Config recorder setup and quantify which resource types would save the most money by switching to daily recording — that requires pulling in your account data though.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
